## In plain English
Directive's hooks inspect shell commands before they run. They decide which tools are shells from one list, `SHELL_TOOL_NAMES`. Claude Code's `PowerShell` tool is not on that list, and the same list builds the hook matcher written into `.claude/settings.json`, so for that tool the hook is either not called or treats the call as an unknown tool. None of the shell guards run: the kill-switch plant guard, the protected-store write guard (`.deft/authz/`, `.deft/approved-scope/`) and the commit-target gate. On 2026-11-21/22, three agents used the PowerShell tool to continue steps a Bash hook had refused.

The guards are written for POSIX shell text, with some PowerShell awareness already, because Cursor's `Shell` tool runs PowerShell on Windows. Adding the name is necessary but may not be enough: PowerShell escapes with a backtick, changes directory with `Set-Location`, and runs programs through cmdlets (`Start-Process`, `Invoke-Expression`, `-EncodedCommand`) that the POSIX readers do not know. The question for this arc is how much PowerShell reading each guard needs, and where the guard should refuse instead of reading.

## Pains
- P1 — Commands sent through Claude Code's `PowerShell` tool bypass every shell-class guard, so an agent can plant a kill-switch flag, write `.deft/authz/` or `.deft/approved-scope/`, or commit into another checkout, by repeating in PowerShell a step a Bash hook refused.
- P2 — Once PowerShell text reaches the guards, PowerShell-only forms escape POSIX reading: a backtick escape inside a flag name (`.no-deft-di` + backtick + `rective` reads as the plain name in PowerShell), `Set-Location <dir>; git commit` (the commit gate knows only `cd`), and program runners (`Start-Process`, `Invoke-Expression`/`iex`, `pwsh -Command`/`-EncodedCommand`, `cmd /c`) that carry a commit or a write as a string. Some of these already affect Cursor `Shell` on Windows.

## Out of scope (named, not pains)
- #6982 (brace expansion before the flag-name test). Built in parallel on the same `classify.ts` region; this arc must compose with it, not reopen it.
- #6959 (glob relief, halted). Its findings stand: quoting does not stop PowerShell wildcard expansion, and programs that run programs defeat allowlists (critic comment 7073921041). This arc grants no new relief.
- #6941 (plain-read relief, merged). Its closed read list already carries `get-content`, `get-childitem`, `get-item`, `select-string`, `test-path`, `gc`, `gci`, `sls`, `set-location`.
- #6740 (honor the kill switch only from a human-minted record) and #7031 (mint audit, which depends on the protected stores staying protected).
- Names built at run time (variables, string concatenation, `[char]` codes, base64): the existing stated limit (`classify.ts` 4041-4042), unless a critic shows PowerShell needs more.

## Anchors at the dispatch SHA
- `packages/core/src/hooks/tools.ts` 41-49: `SHELL_TOOL_NAMES` (Shell, Bash, BashTool, shell, bash, run_terminal_command, monitor); 83-85 `isShellTool`; 262 `SHELL_HOOK_MATCHER = SHELL_TOOL_NAMES.join("|")`.
- `packages/core/src/init-deposit/agent-hooks.ts` 270-290: the matcher deposit and its exact-equality validity check; `packages/runtime/src/setup-wiring.ts` 864; `packages/core/src/init-deposit/host-tool-coverage.ts` 32, 65. This repo's `.claude/settings.json` shell matcher has no `PowerShell`.
- `packages/core/src/hooks/dispatcher.ts` 2075: `shellCommand` is read only when `isShellTool(toolName)`; 2121-2123 the always-on kill-switch plant check; 5130-5146 the shell route (destructive git #3917, dest-forms #3438, launcher family); 5525-5585 `decideProspectiveGitCommitScopeCover` (#6278).
- `packages/core/src/authz/classify.ts` 5957-6005 `classifyHookAuthzOps` (shell branch at 5981; missing command fails open); 6060 `inactiveShellTargetsProtectedStore`; 5194-5260 `INDIRECT_WRITE_BINS` (already lists set-content, out-file, add-content, copy-item, move-item, remove-item, new-item, rename-item, tee-object, pwsh, powershell).
- `classify.ts` 4031-4054 mention rule and `normalizeMentionText` (removes quotes, `\` escapes and cmd `^`; does not remove PowerShell backticks); 4169-4220 `PLAIN_READ_BINS`; 4520-4534 `allSegmentsPlainRead` (any backtick fails the read test); 4536-4554 `mentionRefused` / `hasKillSwitchShellWrite`.
- `packages/core/src/hooks/commit-target.ts` 473-490 wrapper list (no PowerShell runners), 652-673 `readCommand` (`SHELL_BINS` is POSIX shells only), 891-893 `isCdSegment` (only `cd`), 965-990 `resolveCommitTarget`.
- Other `isShellTool` consumers: `hooks/classify/classify.ts` 16, `hooks/classify/tool-name.ts` 85, `hooks/classify/host-session-identity.ts` 571, `coverage-applicability/evaluate.ts` 858.

## Recommended mechanism (the thing to critique)
- R1. Add `PowerShell` to `SHELL_TOOL_NAMES`. Runtime classification and the deposited matcher both change; existing deposits pick it up through the normal repair/upgrade path. Every shell gate then runs on PowerShell-tool commands, as it already does for Cursor `Shell`.
- R2. Kill-switch mention rule: add a normalization variant that removes PowerShell backtick escapes, so a backtick inside a flag name is still a mention. This only adds refusals.
- R3. Protected-store write guard: confirm cmdlet and redirect coverage for both path separators (`Set-Content`, `Add-Content`, `Out-File`, `New-Item`, `Copy-Item`, `Move-Item`, `Rename-Item`, `Remove-Item`, `Clear-Content`, `Tee-Object`, `>`/`>>`, `-Path`/`-LiteralPath`/`-Destination`/`-FilePath`); add any missing writer.
- R4. Commit-target gate: read `Set-Location`, `sl`, `chdir`, `Push-Location` and `pushd` as `cd` (same one-path and `&&` rules, so `;` stays unresolvable); treat PowerShell and cmd program runners (`pwsh`/`powershell` with `-c`/`-Command`/`-EncodedCommand`/`-File`, `cmd /c`, `Start-Process`, `Invoke-Expression`/`iex`, `Invoke-Command`) as commit signals when their text can hold a commit, and as unreadable when it is encoded or expands.
- R5. No blanket refusal: a PowerShell command the readers do not place is judged as it is on Cursor `Shell` today. Reads (`Get-Content`, `Select-String`, `Get-ChildItem`) stay admitted.
- R6. Tests, one per guard through the hook with `toolName: "PowerShell"`: a flag plant, a `.deft/authz/` write and a commit into another checkout are refused; the three reads are admitted.

Questions for the critics:
1. Refutation target: are the POSIX readers plus R2-R4 enough for the PowerShell tool, or does each guard need a PowerShell classifier, or should the PowerShell tool fail closed on any command that mentions a protected name or a commit and is not a closed read? Name concrete one-call escapes.
2. Kill switch: list PowerShell spellings that create or copy a flag file and that the mention rule (with R2) does not see: escapes, `-f` format strings, `+` concatenation, `[char]` codes, `-replace`, `$env:`, wildcard cmdlets (`Copy-Item -Filter`, `Get-ChildItem | Copy-Item`), `.NET` calls (`[IO.File]::WriteAllText`), `Start-Process`, `iex`, `-EncodedCommand`. Which are the stated run-time limit, and which need a rule?
3. Protected stores: what PowerShell writers or path forms (`.deft\authz`, `-LiteralPath`, provider paths such as `FileSystem::`, `$PWD`, `Join-Path`, splatting, `Set-Item`, `.NET` writes) escape `inactiveShellTargetsProtectedStore`?
4. Commit target: does R4 close the PowerShell ways to commit in another checkout (`Set-Location`, `Push-Location`, `-C`, `$env:GIT_DIR`, `Start-Process -WorkingDirectory`, `git.exe`, `& git`), or is "a PowerShell call that changes location and commits is unresolvable" the simpler rule?
5. Blast radius: R1 sends every PowerShell-tool command through every shell gate (launcher family, session ritual, destructive gh verbs, runtimeAuthority push/merge, dest-forms). What ordinary PowerShell work would newly be refused or mis-read? Does changing `SHELL_HOOK_MATCHER` make existing deposits fail a readiness check before repair, and is that acceptable?
6. Composition with #6982 (brace expansion) and #6941/#6959: any order or overlap bug?
7. Does any part add a gate, a refusal class, a verb or a stored file beyond what P1 and P2 need? What is the smallest buildable first slice?

## In plain English

Adding `PowerShell` to the shared tool list is necessary, but R1–R6 do not yet close the described gaps. The proposed changes recognize more commands without fully addressing how PowerShell changes paths and execution state. The smallest defensible design reuses the existing guards and refusal outcomes, with PowerShell-aware handling of protected paths and commit signals.

Short answers to the seven questions:

1. **The proposed extensions are insufficient as written.** A full PowerShell interpreter is unnecessary, but “unknown behaves as Cursor does today” is not evidence of safety. Findings 1–3 identify concrete gaps.
2. **R2 addresses literal backtick obfuscation only.** Format strings, concatenation, character construction, replacement, environment-derived names and encoded payloads remain the declared runtime-construction limit. Literal names inside `.NET` calls or runner strings already meet the mention rule; executable recognition is unnecessary there. Wildcard-copy behavior remains subject to the existing glob rule, without new relief.
3. **Protected-store normalization needs the same attention as flag normalization.** Adding writer names does not repair escaped destination names. Provider paths and computed destinations also need explicit coverage decisions rather than an inference from the writer catalog.
4. **R4 misses environment and location-stack changes.** Refusing a recognized commit whose location cannot be established is simpler than simulating PowerShell state. Plain `git.exe` is already recognized.
5. **Ordinary PowerShell assignments can become commit refusals.** Existing matcher validation also requires exact equality, so old deposits become invalid until repaired. That migration is reasonable if explicitly included and verified.
6. **Composition must preserve the distinction between detecting a protected mention and proving a read.** Backtick removal must not silently grant read relief; #6982 expansion handling and R2 must operate together without replacing each other.
7. **No new verb, stored file or refusal class is needed.** The first slice can change tool registration, conservative PowerShell classification and the existing guard tests. Three happy-path reads and three obvious writes are insufficient evidence for P2.

Verification used source reads at HEAD `65fc6f74abe90c598b05d720d331626c67743dac`, matching the dispatch SHA. No tests or example commands were executed.

## Findings

1. **blocks-the-design — R4 leaves a concrete environment-directed commit targeting the wrong checkout.**

   Evidence: `packages/core/src/hooks/commit-target.ts:236` recognizes POSIX assignment prefixes. Lines 265–272 collect those prefixes only within the Git invocation. Lines 523–525 discard the path prefix before checking whether a command word contains an expansion. Lines 909–932 then inspect only the collected environment names and recognized directory changes, otherwise returning `hook-root`.

   Concrete command:

   ```powershell
   $env:GIT_DIR='C:/other/.git'; $env:GIT_WORK_TREE='C:/other'; git commit -m change
   ```

   These assignment words contain path separators, so the unreadable-command check examines their final path component rather than the `$env:` prefix. They are neither POSIX environment prefixes nor R4 navigation commands. The visible commit can therefore resolve to the hook root while Git uses the other repository. Dispatcher lines 5558–5571 then select the wrong root for scope checking.

   **Disposition consequence:** R4 needs explicit handling of PowerShell mutations of Git location/index environment variables before a commit. Unresolvable is an existing outcome; no new gate is necessary.

2. **blocks-the-design — R2 protects flag mentions but leaves equivalent escaping of approval-store paths untreated.**

   Evidence: `packages/core/src/authz/classify.ts:5033–5034` removes quotes and converts separators, but retains backticks. Lines 5159–5176 match writer tokens against those path spellings. Realpath harvesting at lines 3601–3604 skips expansion-bearing destinations rather than decoding PowerShell escapes.

   Concrete command:

   ```powershell
   Set-Content -LiteralPath ".deft/aut`hz/grants/x.json" -Value '{}'
   ```

   PowerShell removes the backtick before `h`, producing the protected `authz` directory. R3 recognizes `Set-Content`, but the protected-path comparison still receives an escaped spelling. R2 changes only the kill-switch mention normalization. An existing writable grants directory is sufficient for this failure mode; no runtime-built filename is involved.

   **Disposition consequence:** R3 needs PowerShell-aware protected-path normalization or conservative refusal of ambiguous escaped protected paths. Writer enumeration alone cannot substantiate protected-store coverage. Both protected stores need regression cases.

3. **blocks-the-design — R4’s navigation list omits returning through the PowerShell location stack.**

   Evidence: `packages/core/src/hooks/commit-target.ts:891–932` determines location changes solely through `isCdSegment`; R4 proposes additional spellings but omits `Pop-Location` and `popd`.

   Concrete command, when a prior location exists:

   ```powershell
   Pop-Location; git commit -m change
   ```

   PowerShell can commit in the restored checkout while the proposed reader sees no recognized navigation before the commit and selects `hook-root`. The same risk applies to the `popd` alias. This is location state, not filename construction.

   **Disposition consequence:** R4 must include location-stack restoration as an unresolvable commit signal, or explicitly support its state. Refusal is the smaller implementation.

4. **sharpens-framing — R1 activates an existing false commit signal for routine PowerShell assignments.**

   Evidence: `packages/core/src/hooks/commit-target.ts:523–535`, `657–658` and `710–714` treat an expansion-bearing command word as a commit signal without requiring a visible commit. Dispatcher lines 5546–5553 deny an unresolvable result.

   Concrete ordinary read:

   ```powershell
   $text = Get-Content README.md
   ```

   The first word is `$text`, so this assignment can be refused as an unreadable potential commit. This contradicts the broad assurance that ordinary PowerShell reads remain admitted, even though the three bare read examples in R6 pass.

   **Disposition consequence:** Narrow that assurance or include assignment-shaped reads in the admission contract and tests. Any assignment handling must preserve finding 1’s environment protection.

5. **sharpens-framing — Registration repair is part of effective coverage, not merely rollout housekeeping.**

   Evidence: `packages/core/src/init-deposit/agent-hooks.ts:282–288` includes the shared shell matcher among exact-equality matchers; line 914 checks equality. The snapshot’s existing Claude matcher lacks `PowerShell`.

   Updating runtime classification alone leaves an old host registration unable to invoke the hook for that tool. Conversely, validation against the new matcher marks the old registration invalid.

   **Disposition consequence:** The acceptance evidence should include an old-deposit repair case and a representative PowerShell hook payload reaching each guard. The existing repair path is sufficient; no new migration mechanism is justified.

6. **footnote — Conservative lexical extensions remain a reasonable first approach, with bounded claims.**

   The strongest case for R1–R4 is reuse: existing mention detection, protected-store checks, commit-target resolution and refusal outcomes already supply most machinery. A complete PowerShell parser would still not resolve arbitrary runtime computation.

   I would support that smaller approach once the concrete escapes above are covered and ordinary assignment reads have an explicit disposition. This would establish bounded textual protection, not containment of arbitrary agent-generated programs.

```quarantined
role: critic
```

## In plain English

Claude Code's PowerShell tool never reaches Directive's shell guards. The shell list and the matcher deposited in `.claude/settings.json` both omit it, so a command that Bash already refuses still runs when the agent sends it through PowerShell. The tree at `65fc6f74` confirms that gap. Adding the name is the right first move, and the existing POSIX readers can stay. A separate PowerShell parser is the wrong size, and refusing every command that is not a closed read would block ordinary Windows work.

The recommended mechanism still leaves two one-call holes, and it mis-states the backtick case. A PowerShell assignment to `GIT_DIR` or `GIT_WORK_TREE` makes `git commit` land in another checkout while the commit gate treats it as this checkout. A nested `powershell -EncodedCommand` hides a flag plant and a store write from every text scan; the proposal treats that encoding as unreadable only for commits. Backtick handling has to decode PowerShell escapes and join a backtick at the end of a line. The example that puts a backtick before `r` does not create the flag file: in PowerShell that pair is a carriage return.

Question 1. The POSIX readers plus the corrections below are enough. Concrete escapes that survive the text as written: `$env:GIT_DIR = 'D:\other\.git'; git commit`, and `powershell -EncodedCommand` of a plant or a store write.

Question 2. A backtick-newline continuation is one PowerShell command and needs a rule. So does `` `u{hex} `` on PowerShell 7. `` `r ``, `` `n ``, `` `t ``, `` `e ``, `` `f ``, `` `a ``, `` `b ``, and `` `v `` are control characters, not hidden letters. `-f`, `+`, `[char]`, `-replace`, variables, and base64 inside the script stay the limit already stated at `classify.ts` 4041-4042. `Copy-Item -Force` of `*` does not spell a leading-dot name, so it stays in that same limit.

Question 3. `Set-Content`, `Add-Content`, `Out-File`, `New-Item`, `Copy-Item`, `Move-Item`, `Rename-Item`, `Remove-Item`, and `Tee-Object` already count as writers, and a later token is scanned, so `-LiteralPath`, `-Path`, `-Destination`, and a `FileSystem::` prefix are already visible. These still miss: `Clear-Content`, `Set-Item`, the aliases `ac`, `clc`, `si`, and `rni`, `[IO.File]::WriteAllText` / `AppendAllText` / `Copy`, and `Set-Content -Path (Join-Path .deft 'authz\…')`.

Question 4. Once `Set-Location` counts as `cd`, `Set-Location <dir>; git commit` is refused, including a commit in this checkout, because `;` is not `&&`. That refusal is the right close. `git -C <absolute> commit` is the form that still resolves. `Start-Process -WorkingDirectory` is closed only if it is an unreadable signal. `$env:GIT_DIR` is not on the proposed list and still resolves as this checkout.

Question 5. Ordinary `Get-Content`, `Select-String`, and `Get-ChildItem` stay admitted. The new refusals are the plants, store writes, `Set-Location <anywhere>; git commit`, encoded runners, and any backtick inside a `claude` / `grok` / `codex` launch or an exact lifecycle command. Changing the matcher makes every current Claude, Grok, and Codex deposit fail the exact-equality readiness check until repair. That is acceptable only because repair rewrites the deposit. Until that rewrite the host never calls the hook, so the new classifier never sees the tool.

## Problem

Claude Code's `PowerShell` tool is not in `SHELL_TOOL_NAMES` (`packages/core/src/hooks/tools.ts` lines 41-49; the list is Shell, Bash, BashTool, shell, bash, run_terminal_command, monitor), so the kill-switch shell check (#6136) never inspects commands sent through it. On Windows hosts, agents use that tool routinely. Found during the #6959 arc (2026-11-21).

## Acceptance

- `SHELL_TOOL_NAMES` includes Claude Code's `PowerShell` tool, and the kill-switch shell check runs on its commands with PowerShell-aware parsing (or refuses what it cannot parse).
- A test proves a PowerShell-tool command that creates or copies a kill-switch flag file is refused, and an ordinary PowerShell read is admitted.
- Audit every hook check keyed off `SHELL_TOOL_NAMES` (kill-switch plant guard, protected-store write guard for `.deft/authz/` and `.deft/approved-scope/`, commit-target gate) and confirm each now covers the PowerShell tool, with a test per check.

Refs #6136, #6959, #2568.
